tiers.label: Ascended
tiers.definition: Collective perspective. The lyrics speak from, to, or about something larger than any one person.

tenets.text: Subject matter extends beyond self/couple to community, humanity, or the divine
Lyrics articulate universal truth or spiritual reality
Content addresses collective healing, justice, or sovereignty
Lyrics name a systemic or collective condition, not just a personal one
The narrative voice speaks for or to a people, not just "I" to "you"
Lyrics demonstrate surrender to something larger than the self. Not naming it, doing it on the page
Lyrics confront mortality, existence, or the meaning of life as the actual subject, not as metaphor for heartbreak
The song directly challenges a cultural or societal default. Names what's broken and points toward what's whole
Lyrics carry prophetic or testimonial weight. Warning or witnessing beyond the narrator's personal stakes
The song's core message requires collective context. It cannot be reduced to one person's specific experience
Love expressed as universal or collective force, not 1:1 romance
The song gives language to something the culture has no words for. Makes the invisible visible
The song's purpose on the page is selfless. It serves something beyond the narrator

notes.title: Specifics challenge Ascended, not grant it.
notes.text: A song framed as an anthem for a specific identifiable group — by identity, ideology, geography, subculture, faith, or tribe — does NOT auto-qualify for Ascended just because it calls for that group's protection, pride, or liberation. Ascended requires a frequency that transmits universally — one any listener, including those outside the named group, can be elevated by. If a song's elevation is contingent on the listener belonging to (or siding with) the group, its ceiling is Elevated, not Ascended. Test the rule: would a song with the same structure but a different named group — one the listener finds objectionable — still read as transmitting at the highest frequency? If not, it's Elevated. Universal-frequency songs (wisdom, gratitude, pure love, non-group-specific transcendence) still earn Ascended.

tiers.label: Elevated
tiers.definition: Self without ego. Honest internal work on the page. Questioning, accountability, acceptance, processing, growth.

tenets.text: Narrator questions their own assumptions or behavior
Lyrics demonstrate accountability. Owning mistakes, facing consequences
Narrative shows acceptance of a hard truth, not just naming it
The song processes through something with visible movement. Starts one place, ends another
Growth is demonstrated, not just wished for
Lyrics show vulnerability without performance. The narrator is exposed, not curating an image
The narrator confronts their own role in a problem rather than blaming externally
Lyrics contain genuine self-examination. Looking inward with honesty, not self-pity
The song arrives at a perspective earned through the struggle described. Wisdom on the page, not borrowed
The narrator lets go of something: control, resentment, certainty. And it's visible in the lyrics
The narrator demonstrates genuine empathy, forgiveness, or humility on the page. Not as performance, as posture

tiers.label: Decent
tiers.definition: Catch-all. The lyrics don't push in either direction. Pleasant, fun, romantic, sad, nostalgic, but no internal work being done and no ego being served. The song is what it is.

tenets.text: Describes a feeling or situation without developing or moving through it
Tells a story without transformative substance
Expresses 1:1 romance, attraction, or relationship sentiment at face value
Creates atmosphere or mood that doesn't go beyond the feeling itself
Narrator observes or describes but doesn't examine
The song evokes a mood or meets the listener in a feeling, but doesn't move them through it or say something beyond it
The lyrics stay on the surface of a single subject, describing what it looks or feels like without examining what's underneath
The song is pure entertainment or fun with nothing underneath
The song references something deeper but doesn't develop it. Gestures at meaning without delivering
Inspirational or uplifting language without earned substance. "You can do it" without the work behind it

tiers.label: Degraded
tiers.definition: Ego self perspective. The lyrics serve the narrator's ego, promote avoidance, or steer away from growth.

tenets.text: Lyrics celebrate surface-level markers as aspiration. Wealth, status, image, possessions as measures of worth
Narrator frames manipulation or control as romance or love
The song wallows in pain without any movement toward processing
Lyrics promote emotional avoidance or bypassing. Numbing instead of feeling
Content centers the narrator's ego. I'm better, I'm tougher, I deserve more
Lyrics frame self-destructive behavior as strength or identity
The narrator refuses accountability. Blames externally, ignores consequences, or treats responsibility as someone else's problem
Subtle objectification or dehumanization of others, treating people as accessories or conquests
Soft us-vs-them framing. Others are lesser, outside, or beneath the narrator without full contempt
Lyrics feed insecurity or self-doubt as identity rather than something to work through
Lyrics reinforce scarcity, lack, or limitation as the narrator's worldview

tiers.label: Corrupted
tiers.definition: Ego black-hole. The lyrics actively destroy, dehumanize, or consume. Self or others.

tenets.text: Explicit sexual objectification or dehumanization
Lyrics celebrate substance abuse as lifestyle or identity
Promotes violence as entertainment or solution
Contempt for a specific target. Naming, mocking, asserting dominance
Treats possession or control of another person as desirable
Revenge fantasized or celebrated, not processed
The narrator knows something is wrong and leans into it. Self-destruction with open eyes
Lyrics strip dignity from a person or group for entertainment
Glorifies exploitation. Using people, systems, or trust for personal gain
The song's core stance is destruction. Of self, of others, of meaning itself
Total emotional shutdown. Catatonic numbness as the song's stance
Active nihilism. Rejecting meaning, hope, or the sacred
Pure rage as the song's engine. Not processing anger, being consumed by it

modifiers.label: Contaminated
modifiers.definition: **Contaminated** is NOT a separate tier — it is a modifier that can ONLY attach to **violet, blue, or green** songs.
modifiers.body: Red and orange songs CANNOT be contaminated. They already calibrate as harmful — there is no higher-tier substance being undermined. Contamination means a song that meets Decent, Elevated, or Ascended criteria in its overall messaging, but contains specific lines or content that meet Degraded or Corrupted criteria. The song keeps its tier. The contaminating content is flagged separately.
examples: A blue song with real nostalgia contaminated by drug glorification
A violet song with genuine cultural pride but ego woven through the lyrics
A blue song with honest emotional processing alongside objectification
A green song about family with casual glorification of violence
modifiers.closing: Contamination requires the presence of specific lyrical content that meets Degraded or Corrupted tenet criteria. A song that is simply not deep enough to be Elevated is NOT contaminated — it's just Decent.

rules.title: Hyperbolic romantic language is not literal.
rules.text: Hyperbolic romantic language is not literal. "I'd die for you," "risk it all," "sacrifice my life," "swim across the sea" -- these are standard pop romance intensifiers, not evidence of identity erasure or self-abandonment. Unless the lyrics demonstrate ACTUAL loss of self, boundaries, or agency beyond standard devotion language, hyperbolic romance stays in Decent territory. Do not penalize a love song for speaking the way love songs speak.

rules.title: Zero is a specific value, not a fallback.
rules.text: Zero is a narrow, specific score -- not a fallback. 0 means the song's message is precisely centered, with as much elevation as drag and neither side winning, and you can articulate what holds it at center. "Start at zero" is the methodology for where to begin analysis. Landing at zero requires a case. If you cannot decide whether a song reads as high-Decent or low-Decent, resolve the analysis and commit -- do not split the difference at 0. The Decent tier spans the full range between -24 and +24. Use it. Scores like -14, -8, -4, +6, +12, +18 are all valid Decent placements and should land where the song actually sits. Only land at exactly 0 when you can name the equilibrium. Separately, do not default to multiples of 5 or 10 out of habit -- score the value you actually read from the lyrics. If the song lands at -13 or +17, say -13 or +17. Round numbers are not preferred; accurate numbers are.

rules.title: Vocabulary is not substance.
rules.text: Vocabulary is not substance. Naming the sacred — god, spirit, universe, soul, divine — does not activate Ascended tenets. The song must deliver what those tenets require (subject beyond self, universal address, surrender, collective perspective). Test: mentally swap the spiritual noun (god → universe → self). If the activation would change, the activation is vocabulary-driven and should be zero. A song that says 'god' but is structurally a 1:1 transaction does not earn Ascended on vocabulary alone. A song that never names the divine but genuinely delivers collective witness earns it fully. Activation is about what the lyrics do, not what they invoke.

rules.title: Heartbreak distortion vs. predatory control.
rules.text: Heartbreak distortion vs. predatory control. When a song contains both possessive/controlling language AND clear lyrical evidence of grief, loss, or being left, classify the possessive language as distorted heartbreak (Degraded), not predatory intent (Corrupted). Two cases: (a) Clinging-after-loss — the target has already left or is leaving and the surveillance/possession language is the symptom of being unable to release them. Lands in Degraded, severity from high (~-25) to mid (~-50) depending on intensity. (b) Active control over someone present — the narrator threatens, monitors, or asserts ownership over someone still in their orbit, or someone they are trying to keep down. Lands in Corrupted. The test is power: a narrator clinging to an absence has none — they are mourning out loud. A narrator wielding ownership over someone in their orbit has it and is using it. Pathological inability to let go of someone who left is not contempt; it is distorted attachment. Canonical example: "Every Breath You Take" (The Police, 1983). The same song contains "Since you've gone, I've been lost without a trace / I keep crying baby, baby, please" alongside "I'll be watching you / you belong to me." She has gone. The narrator is grieving, not threatening. → Degraded.

rules.title: Narrator perspective: observer/warning vs. first-person endorsement.
rules.text: Narrator perspective: observer/warning vs. first-person endorsement. When a song describes Degraded or Corrupted behavior, the narrator's relational position to that behavior determines tier. Three cases: (a) First-person endorsement — narrator IS the actor, models the behavior as desirable, or invites participation. The dehumanization/objectification/control language activates Degraded or Corrupted tenets at full weight. (b) Observer warning — narrator describes a third party's harmful pattern in cautionary terms, typically third-person ("she", "he", "watch out"), often addressed to another listener. The descriptive language can sound dehumanizing in isolation but the song's stance is warning, not celebrating. Lands Decent (often slightly negative, since cautioning about harm is not uplifting), unless the warning escalates into contempt or diss-track territory. (c) Witness/critique — narrator names harm without enacting it and the song does the work of exposing or counseling around the pattern. Can land Elevated when it processes or transforms (Beat It is an example — warns AND counsels survival). Test: where does the narrator stand relative to the harmful behavior — inside it, warning about it from outside, or critiquing it as a framing? Canonical example: "Maneater" (Hall & Oates, 1983). Narrator is sitting next to another man warning him about a third party who uses men for money. "She-cat," "beast," "maneater" sound dehumanizing in isolation, but the stance is cautionary observer, not endorser — every line is in service of "watch out boy." → Decent (mid-low).

rules.title: Anonymous reading: artist context does not enter the score.
rules.text: A song's score must be derivable from the lyrics on the page. The artist's identity, public reputation, prior catalog, fan-base discourse, marketing positioning, critical reception, and cultural narratives that have grown around them are not evidence and must not influence the calibration. The Compass reads the lyrics, not the persona. This applies in both directions: artist reputation cannot lift a song toward Elevated/Ascended on the strength of perceived sincerity, vulnerability, or depth; nor can it push a song toward Degraded/Corrupted on the strength of perceived persona, genre, or affiliation. Anonymity is the precondition for accurate reading.

rules.title: Demonstrated transformation is the precondition for Elevated.
rules.text: A song earns Elevated tier only when the narrator demonstrates a change in posture, understanding, or state across the lyrics — not when the narrator merely describes self-awareness, vulnerability, or letting-go in static terms. The test is structural: where does the narrator end up materially different from where they began? If the song opens with a description of a state and closes in the same state (however vivid, however self-aware, however articulate), the tier ceiling is Decent. The blue tenets — vulnerability, accountability, processing, letting-go, empathy — measure transformation in motion, not the language of transformation. A narrator who says "I am damaged, I cannot change, here is why" with full clarity is naming a state, not moving through it. Naming earns honesty; movement earns elevation. Without demonstrated movement, even the most articulate self-portrait stays Decent. This rule caps the tier; it does not lower the score within Decent — a vividly honest static self-portrait can still land at the high end of Decent (~+20). Hypothetical, conditional, or wish-form language does not satisfy this rule. Constructions like "I wish I could," "I'd be," "if we found a way," "someday," "if only" are the narrator imagining a different posture, not occupying one. A wish is not a movement. A condition is not a change. The narrator must actually do the thing on the page — actually let go, actually take accountability, actually offer repair without reservation — not name what they would do under different circumstances. If the closing posture relies on subjunctive constructions to claim its transformation, the song stays in Decent. Wishes earn high-Decent at most.

rules.title: Collective ownership of dysfunction is not collective witness.
rules.text: When a song names a systemic, generational, or community-level dysfunction (economic extraction, addiction culture, generational poverty, political apathy, small-town stagnation, etc.) and the narrator's stance toward that condition is ownership, belonging, or identity-claim — "it's ours now," "this is who we are," "welcome to my town" — the song does NOT activate Ascended tenets that reward collective scope (especially tenets 4 and 5), and the systemic naming becomes contamination rather than elevation. The Compass reads collective resignation as collective resignation, not as transformative witness. To activate Ascended on systemic content, the song must demonstrate one of: (a) explicit critique that names the brokenness AND points toward what would be whole, or (b) a narrator who refuses the inherited dysfunction rather than absorbing it as identity. Naming a broken system and then claiming it as home is two negatives, not a positive. Cumulative pattern principle: multiple Degraded signals individually framed as "honest confession" become endorsement when the song's hook claims the catalogue as collective identity. R5 distinguishes endorsement from warning on the Degraded/Corrupted side; R8 makes the parallel distinction on the Ascended side, between critique and absorption.

rules.title: Movement must be the narrator's. Vividness, honesty, and craft are not movement.
rules.text: A song earns Elevated only when the narrator's own posture, internal state, or behavior changes across the lyrics. Movement cannot be demanded of the world, the other person, or circumstances. Imperatives addressed to others ("stay gone," "leave me alone," "come back," "be different"), interrogative requests ("won't you," "can you"), and conditional preconditions ("if you'd just," "when you finally") are wishes directed outward — they describe what the narrator wants from someone else, not a change in the narrator. A wish addressed to another person is still a wish. Aesthetic markers of transformation — vivid imagery, conditional verbs, collective vocabulary, dignified resignation, idealized memory — do not constitute transformation. Vividness is not movement. Honesty is not movement. The presence of craft is not movement. The Compass measures what the narrator does on the page, not what the lyrics perform around the narrator's stasis. If the song's most defensible argument for Elevated relies on stylistic markers rather than a cited change in the narrator, the song stays Decent. R9 is the synthesis cap: when R7 (subjunctive transformation) and R8 (collective ownership) have closed their specific failure modes and a song still finds a narrow band that performs movement without enacting it, R9 names the meta-pattern and holds the tier at Decent.
